We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $\Theta((\varepsilon \beta)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $\beta$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.
papers.authors: Theshani Nuradha, Sujeet Bhalerao, Felix Leditzky

papers.title: In-situ benchmarking of fault-tolerant quantum circuits. I. Clifford circuits
papers.abstract: Benchmarking physical devices and verifying logical algorithms are important tasks for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Numerous protocols exist for benchmarking devices before running actual algorithms. In this work, we show that both physical and logical errors of fault-tolerant circuits can even be characterized in-situ using syndrome data. To achieve this, we map general fault-tolerant Clifford circuits to subsystem codes using the spacetime code formalism and develop a scheme for estimating Pauli noise in Clifford circuits using syndrome data. We give necessary and sufficient conditions for the learnability of physical and logical noise from given syndrome data, and show that we can accurately predict logical fidelities from the same data. Importantly, our approach requires only a polynomial sample size, even when the logical error rate is exponentially suppressed by the code distance, and thus gives an exponential advantage against methods that use only logical data such as direct fidelity estimation. We demonstrate the practical applicability of our methods in various scenarios using synthetic data as well as the experimental data from a recent demonstration of fault-tolerant circuits by Bluvstein et al. [Nature 626, 7997 (2024)]. Our methods provide an efficient, in-situ way of characterizing a fault-tolerant quantum computer to help gate calibration, improve decoding accuracy, and verify logical circuits.
papers.authors: Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail D. Lukin, Michael J. Gullans

papers.title: Interplay between the chiral and deconfinement transitions from a Curci-Ferrari-based Polyakov loop potential
papers.abstract: We couple the two-flavor Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model to a gluonic background corresponding to the gauge-field expectation value in the center-symmetric Landau gauge. Low-energy features in this gauge are captured by a center-symmetric extension of the Curci-Ferrari model and provide a good grasp on key aspects of the confinement/deconfinement transition. Within this framework, we can investigate the interplay between the chiral and deconfinement transitions. Compared to other approaches based on multi-parameter Ans\"atze of the Polyakov loop potential fixed from comparison to finite-temperature lattice data, the modeling of the glue sector in the present set-up depends on only one phenomenological parameter that can be fixed by comparison to lattice data in the vacuum. We detail the structure of the phase diagram, with special emphasis on the finite density axis, and compute thermodynamical observables relevant for applications. We also highlight the properties of the recently introduced net quark number response of the medium as a sensible probe of the phases of QCD, in particular as a tool to disambiguate the nature of certain regions of the phase diagram where the use of the Polyakov loops could lead to misinterpretations. Finally, we critically assess the sensitivity of our results to the various parameters, both in the glue sector and in the chiral sector.
papers.authors: V. Tomas Mari Surkau, Urko Reinosa

papers.title: Virasoro Symmetry in Neural Network Field Theories
papers.abstract: We construct the Virasoro algebra from a neural free-field architecture. A logarithmic momentum law and a smooth spectral window give the weight-one current kernel, whose radial-ordering discontinuity fixes the oscillator pairing. The limiting neural current correlations agree with the Fock vacuum correlations. Their Sugawara stress tensor gives the Virasoro algebra with central charge one, and charged vertex insertions identify its highest-weight sectors. Bounds on regulator and feature errors control finite-mode approximations to this representation. At finite width, an explicit adjoint-compatible projection defines an auxiliary Fock readout when its Hermitian mixed block is positive. Cauchy features extend the construction to fermionic and supersymmetric sectors, including a Clifford zero mode in the Ramond representation, while first-order stress tensors give fermionic and bosonic ghost systems. Shared reflected features impose scalar boundary conditions in every realization and yield conformal and superconformal gluing in the limiting fields. Numerical comparisons support the current pairing and field correlations; their detailed analysis is collected in the appendices.
papers.authors: Brandon Robinson

papers.title: Quantum Nondecimated Wavelet Transform: Theory, Circuits, and Applications
papers.abstract: The quantum nondecimated wavelet transform uses a shift register to apply circular shifts to an amplitude encoded signal before a single orthogonal wavelet transform. We show that tracing out the shift register gives level probabilities equal to the normalized nondecimated wavelet energies, invariant under circular shifts. Its diagonal gives moving averages of squared coefficients. We derive a multinomial model for the level counts and show how to read the autocovariance at lag one for all but the coarsest detail level. For these global statistics, direct Fourier basis measurement of the input is at least as precise and uses a simpler circuit. For denoising, we insert a block encoded shrinkage operator between the transform and its inverse. Postselection on the shift register implements the cycle spinning average exactly as a linear combination of unitaries. Weights shared within each level give a translation equivariant filter with zero phase. Local weights also preserve translation equivariance when indexed by the nondecimated translate. The circuit provides access to individual decimated branches and combines them coherently. We illustrate the method with James Stein shrinkage, local empirical Wiener filtering, and a scaling analysis of turbulent wind velocity. Gate simulations verify the construction, and we report state preparation, weight estimation, and output costs separately.
papers.authors: Brani Vidakovic

papers.title: Full-field-of-view aberration correction for large arrays of focused beams
papers.abstract: We propose and implement an aberration correction method for the creation of extended arrays of spots well beyond the isoplanatic region of any optical system. The method relies on an extensive calibration of aberrations in terms of Zernike polynomials over the full accessible field of an optical system. We introduce a modified Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm for generating holographic phase masks creating fully corrected arbitrary arrays of spots. By applying the method to an aspherical lens, and using a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (SLM), we increase the aberration-free field of view from 50 to 500 $\mu$m, only limited by the largest diffraction angles accessible to the SLM. This opens new perspectives for the generation of large arrays of optical tweezers, especially for neutral atom based quantum processors and simulators.
papers.authors: Yohann Machu, Gautier Creutzer, Cl\'ement Sayrin, Michel Brune

papers.title: Quantum Anticodes
papers.abstract: This work introduces a symplectic framework for quantum error correcting codes in which local structure is analyzed through an anticode perspective. In this setting, a code is treated as a symplectic space, and anticodes arise as maximal symplectic subspaces whose elements vanish on a prescribed set of components, providing a natural quantum analogue of their classical counterparts. This framework encompasses several families of quantum codes, including stabilizer and subsystem codes, provides a natural extension of generalized distances in quantum codes, and yields new invariants that capture local algebraic and combinatorial features. The notion of anticodes also naturally leads to operations such as puncturing and shortening for symplectic codes, which in turn provide algebraic interpretations of key phenomena in quantum error correction, such as the cleaning lemma and complementary recovery. It also yields new descriptions of weight enumerators, including a quantum analogue of Greene's theorem relating weight enumerators to polymatroid invariants.
papers.authors: ChunJun Cao, Giuseppe Cotardo, Brad Lackey

papers.title: Two-dimensional Pulsar Distance Inference from Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
papers.abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are limited in localizing nanohertz continuous gravitational waves (CGWs) by uncertainties in pulsar distances. We introduce a method to infer pulsar distances in two dimensions, using phase information from the pulsar terms of multiple CGW sources. Our approach can enhance distance precision relative to existing one-dimensional distance-inference methods. Using idealized SKA-motivated PTA simulations with prospective pulsar-distance priors, we combine information from five high-SNR CGW sources with known sky positions and luminosity distances. For example, our method achieves subparsec precision for a simulated pulsar at $0.8\,\mathrm{kpc}$ in $40\%$ of realizations, compared with none for the existing one-dimensional method. Such improvements in pulsar-distance precision could facilitate CGW host-galaxy identification and multimessenger observational prospects.
papers.authors: Si-Ren Xiao, Ji-Yu Song, Yue Shao, Ling-Feng Wang, Jing-Fei Zhang, Xin Zhang

papers.title: Many-body $k$-local ground states as probes for unitary quantum metrology
papers.abstract: Multipartite quantum states saturating the Heisenberg limit of sensitivity typically require full-body interactions to be prepared. On the other hand, experimentally practical Hamiltonians often involve few-body correlators only. Here, we study the metrological performances under this constraint, using tools derived from the quantum Fisher information. Our work applies to any encoding generator, also including a dependence on the parameter. For moderate system sizes up to hundred spins (even), we find that symmetric ground states of Hamiltonians with significantly few-body interactions exhibit an average quantum Fisher information that agrees with that of Haar-random symmetric states and displays Heisenberg-like scaling sensitivity. We also discuss the interaction requirements to generate metrologically useful Haar-random symmetric eigenstates. Finally, we establish a tradeoff between the Hamiltonian's gap, which quantifies preparation hardness, and the quantum Fisher information of the corresponding ground state.
papers.authors: Majid Hassani, Mengyao Hu, Guillem M\"uller-Rigat, Matteo Fadel, Jordi Tura

papers.title: Enhancing Kerr-Cat Qubit Coherence with Engineered Dissipation
papers.abstract: Quantum computing crucially relies on maintaining quantum coherence for the duration of a calculation. Bosonic quantum error correction protects this coherence by encoding qubits into superpositions of noise-resilient oscillator states. In the case of the Kerr-cat qubit (KCQ), these states derive their stability from being the quasi-degenerate ground states of an engineered Hamiltonian in a driven nonlinear oscillator. KCQs are experimentally compatible with on-chip architectures and high-fidelity operations, making them promising candidates for a scalable bosonic quantum processor. However, their bit-flip time must increase further to fully leverage these advantages. Here, we present direct evidence that the bit-flip time in a KCQ is limited by leakage out of the qubit manifold and experimentally mitigate this process. We coherently control the leakage population and measure it to be > 9%, twelve times higher than in the undriven system. We then cool this population back into the KCQ manifold with engineered single-photon dissipation, identify conditions under which this suppresses bit-flips, and demonstrate increased bit-flip times up to 3.6 milliseconds. By employing both Hamiltonian confinement and engineered dissipation, our experiment realizes dissipative stabilization of a KCQ. Our results elucidate the interplay between these stabilization processes and indicate a path towards fully realizing the potential of these qubits for quantum error correction.
papers.authors: Francesco Adinolfi, Daniel Z. Haxell, Alessandro Bruno, Laurent Michaud, Venus Hasanuzzaman Kamrul, Preeti Pandey, Alexander Grimm

papers.title: Spectrally Robust Photon-Pair Generation in Topological Waveguide Arrays
papers.abstract: Harnessing topological effects offers a route to protect quantum states of light from imperfections, potentially enabling more robust platforms for quantum information processing. This capability is particularly relevant for active photonic circuits that generate quantum light directly on-chip. However, the impact of topology on the spectral properties of parametric processes, crucial for scalable quantum photonic circuits, remains largely unexplored. Here, we address this question by investigating photon-pair generation via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in nonlinear waveguide arrays, combining experiment and theory. A systematic comparison of uniform, trivial, and topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) arrays reveals that only the topological configuration preserves a stable SPDC resonance spectrum under coupling disorder, with fluctuations in the resonance wavelength reduced by more than an order of magnitude. An analytical model captures the origin of this robustness in the band-structure properties of the interacting modes. Numerical analysis further shows that each SSH array can operate as a robust photon-pair source, enabling stable interference between multiple such sources and the generation of high-dimensional entangled states with high fidelity. These results establish nonlinear waveguide arrays as a promising platform for harnessing the interplay of topology and nonlinearity in quantum photonic circuits.
papers.authors: A. Zecchetto, J. -R. Coudevylle, M. Morassi, A. Lema\^itre, M. I. Amanti, S. Ducci, F. Baboux

papers.title: Noncommutative Gauge Theories: Yang-Mills extensions and beyond - An overview
papers.abstract: The status of several representative gauge theories on various quantum space-times, mainly focusing on Yang-Mills type extensions together with a few matrix model formulations is overviewed. The common building blocks are derivation based differential calculus possibly twisted and noncommutative analog of the Koszul connection. The star-products related to the quantum space-times are obtained from a combination of harmonic analysis of group algebras combined with Weyl quantization. The remaining problems inherent to gauge theories on Moyal spaces in their two different formulations are outlined. A family of gauge invariant matrix models on $\mathbb{R}^3_\lambda$, a deformation of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is presented among which a solvable model. The characterization of 11 new quantum Minkowski space-times through their $*$-algebras is given. A gauge theory of Yang-Mills type is constructed on one recently explored of these space-times and compared to its counterpart built on the popular $\kappa$-Minkowski.
papers.authors: Jean-Christophe Wallet

papers.title: Cyclic universe and uniform rate inflation from polymerized scalar field in loop quantum cosmology
papers.abstract: We investigate the uniform rate inflationary universe in the framework of loop quantum cosmology (LQC) and find that this seemingly simple inflationary model is interlinked with various concepts such as cyclic evolution, HNI inflation, and polymer-quantized scalar fields when the background spacetime is loop-quantized. The potential for an \textit{exactly} uniform rate inflation in a loop-quantized FRW spacetime turns out to be a polymerized version of the corresponding potential in general relativity, which mimics the potentials for a polymerized scalar field and hybrid natural inflation (HNI). There is also a radical modification of the background spacetime, leading to a cyclic universe with identical epochs separated by quantum bounces that replace the classical singularity. The energy density and Hubble rate are bounded. Polymerization of the scalar field is found to be intimately tied to the polymerization of the background geometry in LQC. Remarkably, a single polymerized scalar field simultaneously governs the cyclic evolution of the universe and drives the inflationary phase. Preliminary predictions for cosmological perturbations are worked out and are found to depend on the value of the field at the end of inflation. The parameter space is explored to compare the results for the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio with observational constraints.
papers.authors: Bikash Chandra Paul, Sahil Saini

papers.title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage via Optimized DQI Circuits
papers.abstract: Recently, a quantum algorithm called Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) was introduced that achieves an apparent exponential speedup for Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, which has previously been studied in the contexts of cryptography and error correcting codes. However, this left open the question of how many logical gates and logical qubits would be needed to solve a classically intractable instance of OPI. Here, we develop optimized implementations of DQI which greatly reduce its resource requirements. We establish that DQI for OPI is the first known candidate for verifiable quantum advantage with optimal asymptotic speedup: solving instances with classical hardness $O(2^N)$ requires only $\widetilde{O}(N)$ quantum gates, matching the theoretical lower bound. To realize this, we overcome the primary bottleneck of reversible Reed-Solomon decoding by introducing novel quantum circuits for the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) on degree-$n$ polynomials with $b$-bit coefficients that reduce the leading-order space complexity to $2nb$ qubits. These improvements are broadly applicable, including to Shor's algorithm for the discrete logarithm. We analyze OPI over binary extension fields $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$, assess hardness against new classical attacks, and identify resilient instances. Our resource estimates show that classically intractable OPI instances (requiring $>10^{23}$ classical trials) can be solved with approximately 5.72 million Toffoli gates per shot and $1885$ logical qubits. This is roughly $100$ times fewer gates than required for factoring RSA-2048 and, remarkably, is also less than the leading interactive protocol for computational proof of quantumness, positioning DQI as a compelling candidate for practical, verifiable quantum advantage.
papers.authors: Tanuj Khattar, Noah Shutty, Craig Gidney, Adam Zalcman, Noureldin Yosri, Dmitri Maslov, Ryan Babbush, Stephen P. Jordan

papers.title: Optimal phase change for a generalized Grover's algorithm
papers.abstract: We study the generalized Grover's algorithm with an arbitrary amplitude vector to find the optimal phase change for maximizing the gain in probability for the target of each iteration. In the classic setting of Grover's algorithm with a real initial amplitude vector, we find that a phase change of $\pi$ stays optimal until the probability of observing the target is quite close to 1. We provide a formula for identifying this cut-off point based on the size of the data set. When the amplitude is truly complex, we find that the optimal phase change depends non-trivially on the complexity of the amplitude vector. We provide an optimization formula to identify the required optimal phase change.
papers.authors: Christopher Cardullo, Min Kang

papers.title: A measure on the space of CFTs and pure 3D gravity
papers.abstract: We define a normalizable measure on subspaces of two-dimensional conformal field theories, which we interpret as a maximum ignorance ensemble. These subspaces are specified by a range of allowed central charges and a minimum gap on the scaling dimension of operators. We test whether pure quantum gravity in AdS3 is dual to the average over this ensemble. We find a negative answer, which implies that CFTs with a primary gap of order the central charge are highly atypical in our ensemble. We provide evidence that more generally, holographic CFTs are atypical in the space of all CFTs by finding similar results for permutation orbifolds: subgroups of SN with a good large N limit are very sparse in the space of all subgroups. Along the way, we derive several new results on the space of CFTs. Notably we derive an upper bound on the spacing in central charge between CFTs, which is doubly exponentially small in the large central charge limit.
papers.authors: Alexandre Belin, Alexander Maloney, Florian Seefeld

papers.title: Projected evolution of quantum gates for circuit simulation with matrix product states
papers.abstract: Tensor networks and specifically matrix product states (MPS) enable feasible classical quantum circuit simulation when entanglement remains compressible, but for this, gate updates must balance accuracy, representation size, and runtime. Conventional methods incorporate a complete gate into the MPS before compressing enlarged bonds. Here, we instead use lessons from the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to analyze the projected action of each gate on the MPS by reducing it to a continuous generator path. We establish the spatial and state-space structure of this projected evolution and show that both the fixed-rank and two-site actions are confined to a contiguous window spanned by the gate while retaining boundary information from the surrounding MPS. Within this window characterization, we delineate when the instantaneous two-site action is exact and when variational directions can block it completely. Using standard nearest-point-projection geometry, we also show that fixed-rank TDVP and the local nearest fixed-rank projection of the exact gate endpoint agree to first order. We implement the gate-window restriction with rank-adaptive two-site TDVP and test both the projected update and a hybrid method that reserves it for long-range gates. Across the circuit benchmarks, these implementations incur runtime overhead and show no consistent accuracy--cost advantage over the tested baseline methods. The resulting framework provides a gate-specific structural analysis and a tested implementation together with explicit limits on its practical performance.
papers.authors: Aaron Sander, Maximilian Fr\"ohlich, Mazen Ali, Martin Eigel, Jens Eisert, Michael Hinterm\"uller, Christian B. Mendl, Richard M. Milbradt, Robert Wille

papers.title: On the Spectral Statistics of Multiparametric Random Real Asymmetric Matrices: a hidden universality
papers.abstract: Theoretical analysis of a wide range of complex system e.g. those in contact with environment necessitate consideration of the generic real-asymmetric matrix ensembles, those with varying order of matrix elements e.g. a sparse structure or a banded structure. We pursue the complexity parameter approach to analyze the spectral statistics of the multiparametric Gaussian ensembles of normal real asymmetric matrices and derive the theoretical formulations for the ensemble averaged spectral densities of the real as well as complex eigenvalues. Considerations of the matrix elements with arbitrary choice of mean and variances render us the freedom to model the desired sparsity in the ensemble. Our formulation provides a common mathematical formulation of the spectral statistics for a wide range of sparse real-asymmetric ensembles and also reveals, thereby, a deep rooted universality among them.
papers.authors: Ratul Dutta, Pragya Shukla

papers.title: Influence of dark matter on quantum entanglement and coherence in curved spacetime
papers.abstract: Dark matter (DM) has not yet been directly detected, and phenomenological models such as perfect fluid dark matter (PFDM) provide analytically tractable settings for investigating its possible gravitational effects. Here PFDM denotes the conventional name of an anisotropic effective source, rather than a perfect fluid in the usual isotropic sense. In this work, we study the entanglement and coherence of bosonic and fermionic test fields near a Schwarzschild black hole surrounded by PFDM. These quantum fields probe the background geometry and are not assumed to be microscopic constituents of PFDM. Under our sign convention, only the $\alpha<0$ branch has a positive energy density and carries a physical PFDM interpretation, whereas the $\alpha>0$ branch is retained solely as a formal extension of the same metric family. Within the positive-density PFDM sector, entanglement and coherence vary monotonically with the PFDM parameter, while the complete extended parameter range exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence arising from the corresponding variation of the Hawking temperature. Bosonic entanglement is more susceptible to this geometric effect than fermionic entanglement, whereas fermionic coherence shows a stronger response than its bosonic counterpart. These results characterize how particle statistics and the choice of quantum resource govern the sensitivity of test fields to PFDM-induced modifications of the spacetime geometry.
papers.authors: Shu-Min Wu, Yu-Xuan Wang, Si-Han Shang, Wentao Liu

papers.title: Spacetime-Foam Correlations as the Origin of Cosmological-Constant Dark Energy: Their Effects on Cosmological Evolution and Astrophysical Systems
papers.abstract: Wheeler spacetime foam at the Planck scale is characterized by quantum-gravitational fluctuations that create, oscillate, and annihilate microscopic spacetime structures. We model these structures as a Planck-scale lattice using Euclidean quantum gravity on a simplicial complex. Their long-wavelength collective excitations are described by interacting scalar fields, which we call ``foamons,'' in analogy with phonons in a crystal lattice. Through Coleman--Hawking interactions, foamons couple to quantum or classical field operators at scales much larger than the Planck length. These operators provide physical infrared scales that determine the characteristic correlation lengths of the foamon fields. We use a Wilsonian renormalisation-group framework to study their scaling-invariant behaviour near infrared and ultraviolet fixed points. Integrating out the foamon degrees of freedom generates effective actions for physical field operators, with the foamon correlation lengths setting the corresponding macroscopic scales and effective couplings. We apply this framework to cosmology and astrophysics, where the Ricci-scalar sector gives rise to an effective cosmological term $\Lambda_R\sim\xi_R^{-2}$ with equation of state $p_\Lambda\approx -\rho_\Lambda$. For a cosmological correlation length $\xi_R\sim H^{-1}$, this yields $\rho_{\Lambda_R}\sim M_{\rm pl}^2H^2$, providing a possible mechanism for the small observed dark-energy scale. The effective cosmological term $\Lambda_R$ varies in spacetime and interacts with matter through its dependence on the Ricci scalar. We investigate its effects on cosmic evolution, galactic rotation curves, and the deflection of light grazing the solar surface.
papers.authors: She-Sheng Xue

papers.title: A Modular PyTheus Quantum Network Interpreter: Automated Analysis and Visualization of Optimized Quantum Architectures
papers.abstract: We present a modular interpreter for PyTheus-optimized quantum networks that automatically analyzes and visualizes complex quantum architectures discovered through automated optimization. The interpreter addresses the critical challenge of understanding machine-designed quantum networks by providing robust algorithms for functional role identification, graph-theoretical analysis, and physically meaningful visualization across the major classes of PyTheus-generated networks. Our interpreter accepts both file-based and in-memory network representations, automatically identifies sources, detectors, beam splitters, and ancillas through priority-based classification, and generates coordinated native graph plots and optical table representations. We demonstrate the interpreter's capabilities through two complementary approaches: (1) analysis of a newly developed five-node quantum key distribution network that reveals distributed source architecture and dual-role node functionality, and (2) comprehensive validation using existing PyTheus examples including W4 state generation, heralded Bell state preparation, and GHZ state networks. The interpreter successfully handles complex connectivity patterns across diverse quantum network architectures within the tested classes, avoids visualization artifacts, and provides validation mechanisms for architectural consistency. Our primary contribution is the development of robust modular interpretation algorithms that can analyze the major classes of PyTheus-generated quantum networks, enabling better understanding of automated quantum architecture design.
papers.authors: S. K. Rithvik

papers.title: Simulating and Sampling from Quantum Circuits with 2D Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: Classical simulations of quantum circuits play a vital role in the development of quantum computers and for taking the temperature of the field. Here, we classically simulate various physically-motivated circuits using 2D tensor network ans\"atze for the many-body wavefunction which match the geometry of the underlying quantum processor. We then employ a generalized version of the boundary Matrix Product State contraction algorithm to controllably generate samples from the resultant tensor network states. Our approach allows us to systematically converge both the quality of the final state and the samples drawn from it to the true distribution defined by the circuit, with GPU hardware providing us with significant speedups over CPU hardware. With these methods, we simulate the largest local unitary Jastrow ansatz circuit taken from recent IBM experiments to numerical precision. We also study a domain-wall quench in a two-dimensional discrete-time Heisenberg model on large heavy-hex and rotated square lattices, which reflect IBM's and Google's latest quantum processors respectively. We observe a rapid buildup of complex loop correlations on the Google Willow geometry which significantly impact the local properties of the system. Meanwhile, we find loop correlations build up extremely slowly on heavy-hex processors and have almost negligible impact on the local properties of the system, even at large circuit depths. Our results underscore the role the geometry of the quantum processor plays in classical simulability.
papers.authors: Manuel S. Rudolph, Joseph Tindall

papers.title: Relationship between a $\Phi^4$ matrix model and harmonic oscillator systems
papers.abstract: A Hermitian $\Phi^4$ matrix model with a Kontsevich-type kinetic term is studied. It was recently discovered that the partition function of this matrix model satisfies the Schr\"odinger equation of the $N$-body harmonic oscillator, and that eigenstates of the Virasoro operators can be derived from this partition function. We extend these results and obtain an explicit formula for such eigenstates in terms of the free energy. Furthermore, the Schr\"odinger equation for the $N$-body harmonic oscillator can also be reformulated in terms of connected correlation functions. The $U(1)^N$-symmetry allows us to derive loop equations.
papers.authors: Harald Grosse, Naoyuki Kanomata, Akifumi Sako, Raimar Wulkenhaar

papers.title: Ultracold Mechanical Quantum Sensor for Tests of New Physics
papers.abstract: Initialization of mechanical modes in the quantum ground state is crucial for their use in quantum information and quantum sensing protocols. In quantum processors, impurity of the modes' initial state affects the infidelity of subsequent quantum algorithms. In quantum sensors, excitations out of the ground state contribute to the noise of the detector, and their prevalence puts a bound on rare events that deposit energy into the mechanical modes. In this work, we measure the excited-state populations of GHz-frequency modes in a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator (HBAR). We find that the population of the first excited state can be as low as $P_p$=(1.2$\pm$5.5)$\times10^{-5}$, corresponding to an effective temperature of 25.2 mK, which are upper bounds limited by imperfections in the measurement process. These results compare favorably to the lowest populations measured in superconducting circuits. Finally, we use the measured populations to constrain the amplitude of high-frequency gravitational waves, the kinetic mixing strength of ultra-light dark matter, and non-linear modifications of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation describing wavefunction collapse mechanisms. Our work establishes HBARs as a versatile resource for quantum state initialization and studies of fundamental physics.
papers.authors: Andraz Omahen, Simon Storz, Marius Bild, Dario Scheiwiller, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu

papers.title: Tidal heating effects in binary black hole mergers
papers.abstract: A black hole binary approaching merger undergoes changes in its inspiral rate as energy and angular momentum are lost from the orbits into the horizons. This effect strengthens as the black holes come closer. We use numerical relativity data to model this so-called tidal heating in the strong gravity regime. We present a frequency-domain approximant for nonspinning black hole binaries that accounts for tidal heating effects up to the merger frequency. The approximant includes horizon parameters that characterize the nature of the compact objects. By applying this model to a binary black hole baseline that incorporates tidal heating, one can construct a more accurate point-particle waveform, one that is devoid of finite-size effects of the component objects. We also discuss its ramifications in modeling binary neutron star systems.
papers.authors: Samanwaya Mukherjee, Sayak Datta, Sukanta Bose, Khun Sang Phukon

papers.title: Arbitrary Boundary Conditions and Constraints in Quantum Algorithms for Differential Equations via Penalty Projections
papers.abstract: Complicated boundary conditions are essential to accurately describe phenomena arising in nature and engineering. Recently, the investigation of a potential speedup through quantum algorithms in simulating the governing ordinary and partial differential equations of such phenomena has gained increasing attention. We propose an approach to enforce arbitrary boundary conditions and constraints through adding a penalty projection to the governing equations, relying on known quantum differential equation solvers, leading to an overall efficient quantum algorithm for solving differential equations under boundary conditions and constraints. Assuming a fast-forwardable representation of the projection to ensure an efficient interaction picture simulation, the cost to enforce the constraints is at most $O(\log \lambda)$ in the strength of the penalty $\lambda$ in the gate complexity within the scenarios we considered, for precision $\varepsilon$ and a dynamical system generated by $A_0(t)$ of size $n^d \times n^d$ with forcing $b(t)$. E.g., for the heat equation, this leads roughly to a gate complexity overhead of $\widetilde O(d \log n + \log t)$. We show constraint error bounds for the penalty approach,both constraint and solution error, and provide validating numerical experiments, and estimate the circuit complexity using the Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation.
papers.authors: Philipp Schleich, Tyler Kharazi, Xiangyu Li, Jin-Peng Liu, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Nathan Wiebe

papers.title: Echoes and light rings of regular black holes and their singular counterparts
papers.abstract: Recent work [Phys. Rev. D 111, 104040] showed that the Bardeen and Hayward solutions arise as fine-tuned regular members of broader families that also contain singular black holes. We study massless scalar and auxiliary Maxwell perturbations of these solutions using time-domain evolution and a sixth-order WKB approximation. For part of the singular branch, the time-domain profiles exhibit late-time echoes and the effective potentials develop a double-barrier structure. We also examine null geodesics of the background metric. The same singular branch can have two exterior maxima of the null effective potential separated by a minimum, whereas the type-I regular black holes have a single exterior maximum. The Bardeen and Hayward families display the same qualitative behavior.
papers.authors: Xiao-Pin Rao, Xiao Qian Wang, Hyat Huang

papers.title: Emergent, spacetime-dependent dark energy and gravitational coupling from moving geometries
papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of moving Cartan geometries described by quotients of Lie groups and Lie algebras with spacetime dependant structure constants and construct associated deformed topological gauge action functionals for Lorentzian (including dS and AdS) and Lorentz$\times$Weyl moving geometries. The actions feature a generalization of the Nieh-Yan topological term for a varying coupling constant. We compute the equations of motion of the gauge $+$ matter actions and show that they dictate at each spacetime point the geometry, leading to both a spacetime-dependent source of dark energy and gravitational coupling, described by combinations of scalars built from spacetime curvature, torsion and the matter content of the theory. The action becomes asymptotically topological when the gauge action contribution to dark energy vanishes.
papers.authors: Jean Thibaut

papers.title: Atoms, Worldlines, and the Scalar Approximation
papers.abstract: The worldline path-integral method, developed thus far for scalar fields, offers promising computational efficiency in general geometries, However, it relies so far on the scalar approximation that decomposes electromagnetic waves into two independent polarizations. In this work, we investigate different theoretical frameworks of fluctuation-induced effects and analyze the limitations of the worldline path-integral method in modeling multiple-atom Casimir-Polder interactions. In particular, we ask the question: how accurate is the scalar approximation? Using the worldline approach, it appears that a simple sum of the contributions from the two polarizations agrees with the exact Casimir-Polder force for two-atom systems. However, it turns out that this agreement is fortuitous. To enable calculations beyond two atoms via worldlines, we develop general N-atom expressions for the Casimir-Polder force within the scalar approximation. For three-body systems, the scalar worldline method fails drastically, predicting significant discrepancies in both magnitude and sign due to strong polarization mixing. Furthermore, we show that the TE/TM decomposition in the worldline method differs from that of the Green-tensor formalism, and we discuss why this is. This study highlights the inadequacy of scalar worldline models that rely on the polarization-decomposition approximation in general geometries.
papers.authors: He Zheng, Daniel A. Steck

papers.title: Jordan-H\"older property for shifted quantum affine algebras
papers.abstract: We prove that finite length representations of shifted quantum affine algebras in category $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{sh}}$ are stable by fusion product. This implies that in the topological Grothendieck ring $K_0(\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{sh}})$ the Grothendieck group of finite length representations forms a non-topological subring. We also conjecture this subring is isomorphic to the cluster algebra discovered in arXiv:2401.04616. In the course of our proofs, we establish that any simple representation in category $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{sh}}$ descends to a truncation, for certain truncation parameters as conjectured in arXiv:2010.06996 in terms of Langlands dual $q$-characters.
papers.authors: David Hernandez, Huafeng Zhang

papers.title: Dressed Subsystems in Classical Gravity
papers.abstract: This paper considers the problem of consistently defining subsystems in gravitational theories. It is argued that a subsystem is a spacetime subregion in which the observables form a closed Poisson algebra. In a generally covariant theory, the location of the subregion must be determined in relation to other degrees of freedom. It is proposed that these degrees of freedom should live within the region, so that an observer can determine its edge by only measuring fields inside of it. This turns out to be equivalent to the property that observables in the subregion generate field-dependent gauge transformations on the causal complement. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this is \textit{exactly} what is necessary for the observables to form a Poisson algebra and thus to constitute a consistent subsystem. Observables in spacelike separated "dressed subsystems" are shown to commute. Several examples are given in the context of General Relativity. Along the way, new perspectives on the covariant phase space formalism are introduced that clarify well-known issues, such as the factorization of subregions in gauge theories and the unambiguous definition of Noether charges associated with one-sided boosts. Finally, prospects for extending these results to a perturbative quantum setting are discussed.
papers.authors: Pranav Pulakkat

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Quantum Error Correction: A Comprehensive Review
papers.abstract: Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is the process of detecting and correcting errors in quantum systems, which are prone to decoherence and quantum noise. QEC is crucial for developing stable and highly accurate quantum computing systems, therefore, several research efforts have been made to develop the best QEC strategy. Recently, Google's breakthrough shows great potential to improve the accuracy of the existing error correction methods. This survey provides a comprehensive review of advancements in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to enhance QEC schemes for existing Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. Specifically, we focus on machine learning (ML) strategies and span from unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, to reinforcement learning methods. It is clear from the evidence, that these methods have recently shown superior efficiency and accuracy in the QEC pipeline compared to conventional approaches. Our review covers more than 150 relevant studies, offering a comprehensive overview of progress and perspective in this field. We organized the reviewed literature on the basis of the AI strategies employed and improvements in error correction performance. We also discuss challenges ahead such as data sparsity caused by limited quantum error datasets and scalability issues as the number of quantum bits (qubits) in quantum systems kept increasing very fast. We conclude the paper with summary of existing works and future research directions aimed at deeper integration of AI techniques into QEC strategies.
papers.authors: Zihao Wang, Hao Tang

papers.title: Kerr-Induced Impairments in Quantum-Classical Fiber Coexistence: A Quantum-Stochastic Analysis
papers.abstract: Quantum and classical optical signals sharing a fiber can interact through Kerr cross-phase modulation without interchannel photon transfer, potentially degrading phase- and mode-sensitive quantum communication even when direct spectral leakage is negligible. We develop a two-channel quantum-stochastic propagation framework based on the positive-P representation for a weak coherent pulse train co-propagating with a strong, quadrature-amplitude-modulated classical signal. Both fields are treated quantum mechanically, incorporating self- and cross-phase modulation, chromatic dispersion, group-velocity mismatch, attenuation, and Kerr-induced quantum diffusion. We characterize the classical-channel influence using three complementary observables: the frequency-resolved quadrature-fluctuation spectrum, complex temporal-mode overlap, and adjacent-pulse interference visibility. Simulations of a 100-km standard-fiber link reveal markedly different responses across these observables. As classical launch power increases, the extremal quadrature-fluctuation spectra remain close to the shot-noise level, whereas the temporal-mode and visibility penalties reach approximately 4.5% and 6.0%, respectively, at 100 mW. Applying a 1% mean-penalty criterion gives launch-power thresholds of approximately 46 mW for temporal-mode overlap and 40 mW for visibility, yielding a joint Kerr-limited threshold near 40 mW for the investigated configuration. These results demonstrate that temporal-mode deformation and reduced pulse-to-pulse coherence can occur while the evaluated quadrature-fluctuation spectra remain near shot noise, establishing a complementary criterion for selecting classical launch power in quantum-classical fiber co-propagation.
papers.authors: Sumit Chaudhary, Shahram Dehdashti, Igor Litvin, Janis N\"otzel

papers.title: Symmetries, correlation functions, and entanglement of general quantum Motzkin spin-chains
papers.abstract: Motzkin spin-chains, which include `colorless' (integer spin $s=1$) and `colorful' ($s \geq 2$) variants, are one-dimensional (1D) local integer spin models notable for their lack of a conformal field theory (CFT) description of their low-energy physics, despite being gapless. The colorful variants are particularly unusual, as they exhibit power-law violation of the area-law of entanglement entropy (as $\sqrt{n}$ in system size $n$), rather than a logarithmic violation as seen in a CFT. In this work, we analytically discover several unique properties of these models, potentially suggesting a new universality class for their low-energy physics. We identify a complex structure of symmetries and unexpected scaling behavior in spin-spin correlations, which deviate from known 1D universality classes. Specifically, the $s=1$ chain exhibits $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order. Meanwhile, the $s \geq 2$ chains do not appear to spontaneously break any symmetries, but display quasi-long-range algebraic order with power-law decaying correlations, inconsistent with standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical exponents. We also derive asymptotic scaling expressions, with explicit additive constants, for entanglement measures in both colorless and colorful chains, generalizing previous results of Movassagh [J. Math Phys. (2017)], while providing benchmarks for potential quantum simulation experiments. The $\sqrt{n}$ entanglement scaling implies that any matrix-product-state description of these ground states requires bond dimension $e^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$; this superpolynomial cost of the standard 1D tensor-network toolkit, along with the analytical tractability of their ground state properties, positions Motzkin spin chains as intriguing testbeds for quantum simulation of many-body physics.
papers.authors: Varun Menon, Andi Gu, Ramis Movassagh

papers.title: On co-dimension 2 defect anomalies in N=4 SYM and (2,0) theory via brane probes in AdS/CFT
papers.abstract: We consider a half-BPS solution for a D3 brane probe in AdS$_5 \times S^5$ that has world-volume geometry of AdS$_3 \times S^1$. It intersects the boundary over a surface that represents a dimension 2 defect in the boundary ${\cal N}=4$ SYM theory. The effective action of the probe brane is proportional to the logarithmically divergent volume of AdS$_3$ and may thus be interpreted as computing conformal anomaly of supersymmetric $S^2$ defect. The classical action scales as $N$. We compute the 1-loop correction to it due to quantum fluctuations of the D3 brane world-volume fields and compare the result to an earlier suggested expression for the defect anomaly. With the boundary condition for the zero mode of the world-volume vector required by supersymmetry the sum over the modes gives the 1-loop coefficient $-3$ instead of the expected $-6$. We suggest that the remaining part is due to the classical response of the background to the probe. We also perform a similar analysis of a half-BPS supersymmetric M5 brane probe solution in AdS$_7 \times S^4$ with the world-volume geometry of AdS$_5 \times S^1$ that represents a dimension 4 defect in the boundary (2,0) 6d theory. Here the classical M5 brane action computes the leading order $N^2$ term in $a$-anomaly of the supersymmetric $S^4$ defect. The fluctuations form a tower of chiral multiplets and a flavour current multiplet of the 4d ${\cal N}=2$ superconformal symmetry. We perform a detailed computation of the 1-loop correction to the M5 brane effective action and discuss prescription dependence of the prediction for the contribution to the $S^4$ defect $a$-anomaly coefficient.
papers.authors: Hongliang Jiang, Arkady A. Tseytlin

papers.title: Nonabelian mirrors and Gromov-Witten invariants
papers.abstract: We propose quantum differential equations (QDEs) for periods of nonabelian mirror theories and develop an algorithm for constructing them directly from the mirrors. We verify the proposal by recovering known quantum differential equations of Grassmannians and Picard-Fuchs equations of Calabi-Yau complete intersections in Grassmannians. Our algorithm applies to a broad class of nonabelian GLSMs and yields new examples of quantum differential equations for several Fano varieties. The associated cohomology-valued generating functions can be extracted directly from these equations. Using them, we compute instanton numbers of both complete-intersection and non-complete-intersection Calabi-Yau manifolds, including the Pfaffian and Gulliksen--Neg{\aa}rd Calabi-Yau threefolds. The resulting instanton numbers agree with all previously known computations, while the generating functions obtained for the non-complete-intersection examples are new.
papers.authors: Wei Gu, Jirui Guo, Yaoxiong Wen

papers.title: Quadratic Models for Engineered Control of Open Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework to model the evolution of a class of open quantum systems whose environments periodically undergo an instantaneous non-unitary evolution stage. For the special case of quadratic models, we show how this approach can generalise the formalism of repeated interactions to allow for the preservation of system-environment correlations. Furthermore, its continuous zero-period limit provides a natural description of the evolution of small systems coupled to large environments in negligibly perturbed steady states. We explore the advantages and limitations of this approach in illustrative applications to thermalisation in a simple hopping ring and to the problem of initialising a qubit chain via environmental engineering.
papers.authors: J. P. P. Vieira, A. Lazarides, T. Ala-Nissila

papers.title: Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling
papers.abstract: The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.
papers.authors: Zhiqian Su

papers.title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
papers.abstract: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(\lambda^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $\lambda$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(\lambda^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.
papers.authors: Ji-Hui Pei, Jin-Fu Chen

papers.title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
papers.abstract: We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied to the ions. In addition, we demonstrate individual addressing of dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal.
papers.authors: Ivan A. Boldin, Elham Esteki, Bogdan Okhrimenko, Friederike Giebel, Konstantin Thronberens, Amado Bautista-Salvador, Christian Ospelkaus, Christof Wunderlich

papers.title: Beyond hidden zeros and uniqueness in Tr$(\phi^3)$: Block and rod zeros in any Tr$(\phi^m)$
papers.abstract: Hidden zeros have proven powerful tools for reconstructing amplitudes in Tr$(\phi^3)$, a theory of colored scalars with cubic interactions. We show that these structures extend to any Tr$(\phi^m)$ theory. For odd $m$, we construct \emph{block zeros} from orthogonal sums of consecutive momenta, generalizing the original cubic hidden zeros. For every $m\geq4$, including even $m$, we describe a second family of nonlinear \emph{rod zeros} through a rod packing problem. In Tr$(\phi^4)$ this construction reduces to a simple rank-one condition on a matrix of momentum contractions. We connect this new zero to the classic threshold nullification zeros of Voloshin, where certain amplitudes in massive $\phi^4$ theory vanish when all produced particles are at rest. Finally, we demonstrate the reconstruction power of these zeros. Assuming locality, we prove that the rod zeros uniquely fix all Tr$(\phi^m)$ tree amplitudes for $m\geq4$ up to normalization. We also conjecture that the block zeros enforce both locality and unitarity for any Tr$(\phi^m)$ theory with odd $m$.
papers.authors: Laurentiu Rodina

papers.title: Efficient search for microlensed gravitational-wave signals with matched filtering and a two-image statistic
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences can be microlensed by compact objects along the line of sight, producing frequency-dependent waveform distortions. As standard matched-filter searches rely on unlensed templates without accounting for lensing effects, microlensed signals can lose signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) through template mismatch and suffer further losses from signal-consistency tests. We quantify both effects for the $\texttt{PyCBC}$ search using microlensed injections in simulated data. The two losses occupy different regions of lens parameter space in the geometric optics representation: template mismatch is governed by the relative magnification of the two images, while the consistency-test penalty is governed by their time delay. We show that a microlensed signal lies in the two-dimensional subspace spanned by a template and its time-shifted copy, allowing the relative magnification and Morse phase to be maximized over analytically, leaving only the time delay to search. The resulting statistic requires no extension of the template bank and reduces the median loss in re-weighted SNR from $10\%$ to $1.6\%$, and the $90^\mathrm{th}$ percentile from $41\%$ to $9\%$. At a false-alarm rate of one per day, the relative detection volume improves by about $6\%$ across all injections, and by a factor of $1.9$ for the $10\%$ of injections most affected by lensing. In addition to increased detection capacities, we also show how the detection statistic can be used to establish the lensed nature of the trigger. Therefore, the work proposed here lays the foundation for an effective search and identification of microlensed signals in gravitational-wave data.
papers.authors: Soumen Roy, Justin Janquart

papers.title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.
papers.authors: Sahinur Reja

papers.title: CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation
papers.abstract: Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.
papers.authors: Wenjie Sun, Xiaoyu Li, Zhigang Wang, Yuchen He, Shengbin Wang, Hantao Sun

papers.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
papers.abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.
papers.authors: Aleksei V. Ivanov, Christoph S\"underhauf, Jon Kunjummen, Nick S. Blunt, R\'obert Izs\'ak

papers.title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
papers.abstract: How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $\epsilon$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cram\'er--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.0451$ for direct measurement and $0.0295$ with exact shares.
papers.authors: Brani Vidakovic

papers.title: From geometric curvature to effective backgrounds: a dictionary for Dirac fermions in one, two and three spatial dimensions
papers.abstract: Dirac equation on curved backgrounds can be rewritten as a flat-space equation in which geometry appears as a tensorial Fermi velocity together with a set of background fields. We derive this correspondence from a single Clifford-algebra identity and follow it through one, two, and three spatial dimensions. Once the spin connection is written in terms of Ricci rotation coefficients, only two contractions can occur. The trace produces a term with the index structure of a vector potential in every dimensionality; it enters with an imaginary factor i and is precisely the term that keeps the operator Hermitian when the Fermi velocity depends on position. The totally antisymmetric contraction produces an object that depends on the number of indices available to the Levi-Civita symbol: a trace on a line, a pseudoscalar mass on a surface, and an axial vector potential in a volume. Neither contraction is invariant under local rotations of the frame, and we give the transformation laws. On a surface, the curl of the trace term can always be removed by a frame rotation, while its divergence is proportional to the Gaussian curvature. We apply the correspondence to a Gaussian bump, where the local density of states at the center falls below its flat value and obeys a closed form at low energy; to a wire, where a nonuniform lapse binds states inside the gap and a nonuniform velocity cannot; to stationary frames on a surface, where a circulating drag shifts the Dirac mass locally with either sign; and to twisted and rotating frames in a volume, where the axial term takes the form of a chiral chemical potential produced by the frame alone, or separates Weyl nodes in a rotating sample. We separate the geometric contribution from the lattice pseudogauge field that dominates the response of strained samples
papers.authors: David Valenzuela, Alfredo Raya

papers.title: Rotating black hole thermodynamics at NNLO in higher-curvature gravity
papers.abstract: We investigate higher-curvature corrections to black-hole thermodynamics in quasitopological gravity using perturbative Euclidean-action methods. Static, spherically symmetric black holes provide a benchmark for the action expansion, while our main application concerns five-dimensional, asymptotically flat, rotating black holes with equal angular momenta. For Einstein gravity supplemented by Gauss--Bonnet and cubic quasitopological interactions, we compute the Gibbs free energy through next-to-next-to-leading order, retaining both quadratic and cubic corrections. The result retains the full dependence on the background spin parameter, without a slow-rotation expansion, and extends to arbitrary couplings of quadratic and cubic curvature invariants. We derive the corrected mass, entropy and angular momenta, and show how rotation affects the size and sign of the corrections.
papers.authors: Cristobal Laporte

papers.title: Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters
papers.abstract: We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.
papers.authors: Adri\'an Juan-Delgado, Diego Mart\'in-Cano, Paloma A. Huidobro

papers.title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
papers.abstract: Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.
papers.authors: Lloren\c{c} Balada Gaggioli, Jakub Mare\v{c}ek

papers.title: Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons
papers.abstract: Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.
papers.authors: Sunjun Hwang, Leong Chuan Kwek

papers.title: Whitehead doubles and the failure of the AJ conjecture
papers.abstract: For marked Whitehead doubles of torus knots with coprime parameters $2\le r<s$, the AJ conjecture fails for both clasp signs, both companion chiralities, and every integer twist. The zero-framed signed unreduced colored Jones sequence has a nonzero rationally saturated annihilator. Every nonzero primitive representative specializes nontrivially at $t=-1$ with the meridian variable $M$ independent. With $L$ the longitude variable, the specialization contains the irreducible quadratic $E=L^2-(M^4-4M^2+1)L+M^4$ for the negative clasp and $M^4E(M^{-1},L)$ for the positive clasp. The corresponding quadratic is coprime to the full classical $A$-polynomial, including $L-1$, over $\mathbb{Q}(M)[L^{\pm1}]$, so the discrepancy persists when each irreducible factor is counted once. The curve $E=0$ comes from the marked Whitehead link exterior with its axis cusp complete. For the displayed monic polynomial, $\pi m(E)$ is the unsigned volume of that two-cusped exterior. We use the actual Jones sequence to select a right divisor of the satellite transfer operator. Rational factor tests show that the quadratic survives in this divisor, and the two marked companion fillings exclude it as a component of the satellite boundary curve.
papers.authors: Jinzheng Li, Yuqi Li, Hao-Yu Sun

papers.title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
papers.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.
papers.authors: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli

papers.title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms
papers.abstract: The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.
papers.authors: J. C. Bellizotti Souza, M. C. de Oliveira

papers.title: Holography at finite resolution: zero-point length in AdS/CFT
papers.abstract: We explore the zero-point length $l_0$ of T-duality-inspired effective field theory in holography, distinguishing two readings. As a boundary resolution scale, $l_0$ filters the source of a bulk scalar in anti-de Sitter space and yields an exactly solvable boundary response that is ultraviolet finite without a hard cutoff and inherits the power-law tails of the zero-point-length kernel. We show that this filter is the source-normalized bulk-to-boundary transfer function of a $\nu=1$ scalar evaluated at radial depth $z=l_0$. Anchoring Ryu-Takayanagi surfaces on the same radial surface gives finite entanglement entropies that retain the perimeter law and the universal sphere free energy.
